name: Soka senbei (Soka rice cracker)
text: Hard-baked, soy-sauce-flavoured senbei from Soka, Saitama, made from non-glutinous (uruchi) rice. The local tradition is tied to Soka-juku, a post town on the Nikko Kaido in the Edo period, where the preserved snack began to be sold. It was first called shio-senbei (salt senbei) to distinguish it from sweet sugared senbei. Registered as a regional collective trademark in 2007; rights holder was the Soka Senbei Kyodo Kumiai.
flavor: Hard, crisp bite with a toasted-rice aroma and a direct soy-sauce savour; the shoyu-basted surface is the main seasoning.
use: Eaten as a tea snack and sold as a souvenir; also taken as a hand-baking experience in Soka. Sold plain-shoyu or in flavoured variants by individual makers.
craft: Process as described by local sources: rice is milled to flour, steamed, pounded into a mochi-like mass, then shaped and baked. The certification standard asks for baking in a pressed-tile (oshi-gawara) mold or a hard-baked product that adopts the oshi-gawara method. Sun-drying and hand-baking are still done at some bakeries while other steps are mechanised. Sources disagree on how many makers exist (about 40 vs more than 60) and on the later merger of the baking guilds into the Soka Senbei Promotion Council, so check the current body before quoting.

name: Senbei, okaki and arare (rice cracker categories)
ja: せんべい・おかき・あられ
text: Common classification of Japanese rice crackers by raw rice. Senbei is made from ordinary non-glutinous uruchi rice (the table rice); okaki and arare are made from glutinous mochigome. Okaki and arare differ mainly by size, with no numeric standard; one explanation puts 5 cm or more as okaki and smaller as arare. Okaki traces to kakimochi, pieces of broken kagami mochi; one theory has arare starting from roasted glutinous rice.
flavor: Senbei: firm, crunchy, rice-flavoured. Okaki/arare: lighter, puffed, crisp-melting texture from glutinous rice.
use: Used in speech and on labels to sort rice crackers; for purchasing, check the ingredient list (mochigome vs uruchi rice) rather than the name.
craft: The distinction is by ingredient, not by shape. Sources consulted show that boundaries between okaki and arare vary by company and explanation, and the industry association's own definition did not appear in the search results. Treat size thresholds as convention.

name: Kakinotane (Nagaoka, crescent-shaped rice cracker)
text: Crescent-shaped, soy-sauce-flavoured rice cracker said to have originated at Naniwaya Seika in Nagaoka, Niigata. Naniwaya, which made arare in oval (koban) molds, is said to have found the shape when the founder's wife crushed a mold in 1924, and kept using the crescent mold; the shape resembled a persimmon seed. Dates differ by source (1924 in Naniwaya-related accounts, 1925 in Wikipedia; company founding given as 1919 or 1923). It was not trademarked and the method was disclosed, so many makers entered and the name became generic.
flavor: Crisp small cracker with soy sauce savour.
use: Snack and drinking accompaniment; Naniwaya promotes Nagaoka as the birthplace. Kameda Seika, also from Niigata, holds the top domestic share per Wikipedia.
craft: The product is a lesson in naming and IP: no trademark meant it is a generic category. When citing origin, give the date range rather than a single year, since sources conflict. Naniwaya Seika is the maker usually cited as the original.

name: Karinto (fried flour sticks with sugar coating)
text: Deep-fried flour sticks coated in melted sugar, classified as a fried confection and a dry confection (higashi). Sources give a theory of arrival in the Nara period via Tang confections, but the Edo accounts are firmer: in the Tenpo era, Yamaguchi-ya Kichibei (name as read from the Japanese source) of Fukagawa sold it as hana-rinto; in 1875 the Iida-ya of Asakusa Nakamise sold black-sugar-coated sticks, regarded as the source of the present form.
flavor: Crunchy interior, sweet, molasses-like coating when brown sugar is used.
use: Tea snack; brown sugar (kokuto) coating is the standard, white sugar versions also exist.
craft: Basic route: knead flour with sugar, water, salt and a leavening agent, shape into sticks, fry, coat with boiled-down brown or white sugar, dry. Sources consulted did not give frying temperatures or the trade association's standards; brown sugar was cheaper than white, which is cited as a reason for its adoption.

name: Taiyaki (sea-bream-shaped cake)
text: Bean-paste-filled batter cake baked in sea-bream-shaped molds. Tradition credits Naniwaya Sohonten in Azabu-Juban, Tokyo, founded in 1909 (Meiji 42): the first owner reportedly sold imagawayaki without success, a turtle shape also failed, and the sea bream (tai) shape sold. This account rests on Tabemono Kigen Jiten, so treat it as tradition. One source notes taiyaki can only be traced back to the Meiji era.
flavor: Crisp thin shell, sweet filling; classic filling is sweet bean paste.
use: Street snack, eaten hot from the mold.
craft: The taiyaki and imagawayaki are the same family of mold-baked batter cakes; the shape is the difference. Origin claims differ between sources.

name: Imagawayaki / obanyaki / kaitenyaki / Gozasoro
ja: 今川焼き・大判焼き・回転焼き・御座候
text: Round bean-paste cakes baked in a mold, with regional names. Imagawayaki is the oldest name, connected to the Imagawabashi area of Edo; the earliest record is cited as the 1777 ranking booklet Fukichi-za-i, and it spread mainly in the Kanto region from the mid-Edo period. Obanyaki became common from the Meiji era, and kaitenyaki in the Kansai. Gozasoro was originally a company product name from Himeji, Hyogo, post-war, and spread as a generic term in the region. A university column ranked obanyaki first, imagawayaki second and kaitenyaki third in a survey of usage.
flavor: Soft pancake-like shell, sweet bean paste filling.
craft: Dating conflicts between sources (some place obanyaki in the Edo period, others in the Meiji era). Name choice is itself a regional marker, so ask the local term before labelling.

name: Shiroi Koibito (Ishiya, Sapporo)
text: Sapporo souvenir sweet by Ishiya Seika: chocolate sandwiched between langue-de-chat cookies. Launched in December 1976. The name is reported to come from a remark by the founder, and one source links it to the Japanese title (Shiroi Koibitotachi) of the documentary film on the 1968 Grenoble Winter Olympics; the sources describe that link as the likely origin rather than a documented fact.
flavor: Thin crisp cookie with a smooth chocolate filling.
craft: Sources seen cover brand history and trademark; they do not give formula or process data.

name: Hagi no Tsuki (Sendai souvenir cake)
text: Sendai souvenir confection by Kasho Sanzen. Its development is tied to the opening of the Sendai-Fukuoka air route in 1978, when the company aimed for an in-flight sweet; its main product Date Emaki was not chosen but the new Hagi no Tsuki was. The launch year differs across sources (1977 and 1979 both appear).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
craft: Sources seen do not give composition or process. Check the maker for details before quoting a launch year.

name: Tokyo Banana
text: Tokyo souvenir banana-flavoured sweet launched in 1991 under the product name Mitsuketa. Sold by Grapestone; manufactured under OEM by Masudac of Tokorozawa, Saitama. Banana was chosen to appeal to all ages.
craft: Sources seen do not give process detail. Note the split between seller (Grapestone) and maker (Masudac).

name: Hakata Torimon
text: Fukuoka souvenir manju made by Meigetsudo of Hakata-ku. White bean paste wrapped in a flour dough; cream and butter are used, giving a Western-confection character. Launched in 1993 per the maker's pages (shop page: 8 March 1993), though sources vary on timing.
flavor: Milky, butter-rich white bean paste, soft skin.
craft: The cream and butter in the filling are what separate it from a standard white-an manju. Check launch date against the maker.

name: Marusei Butter Sand (Rokkatei)
ja: マルセイバターサンド
text: Rokkatei's butter sandwich cookie from Obihiro, Tokachi, released on 14 May 1977, the same day the company changed name from Chiaki-an Obihiro branch to Rokkatei. The name comes from Marusei Butter made by Banseisha, founded by Yoda Benzo; Banseisha's butter in 1905 is cited as the first commercial butter in Hokkaido. Rokkatei produced Japan's first white chocolate in 1968, and Wikipedia says that success helped lead to the sandwich.
flavor: Butter cream with raisin, crisp biscuit.
use: Hokkaido souvenir, also everyday sweet in Tokachi.
craft: The name is a deliberate nod to the Banseisha butter. Sources seen do not give recipe ratios or process.
src: Mynavi News: Rokkatei Marusei Butter Sand

name: Okinawa zenzai (shaved-ice zenzai)
text: In Okinawa, zenzai is a cold dish: kintoki beans simmered sweet and plump with sugar or brown sugar, topped with a mound of shaved ice. According to Ryukyu Cuisine Preservation Association's Yasutomi Junko (as reported by Ryukyu Shimpo), it is rooted in the prewar azuki zenzai; ice was added some time after the war.
flavor: Sweet soft beans against cold ice.
craft: Different from mainland zenzai (hot azuki soup). The beans are kintoki beans, as the source describes.

name: Beni-imo tart (Yomitan)
text: Tart filled with purple sweet potato paste. Born in 1986 (Showa 61) in Yomitan village, where villagers began making sweets with the local beni-imo as part of a village revitalisation campaign. The sweet potato is traditionally said to have been brought from China in 1605 by Noguni Sokan.
craft: Local sourcing was the point of the movement. Sources seen give no process detail.

name: Hanabooru (Ryukyu baked cookie)
text: Baked confection in the Ryukyu repertoire. Per ALIC, hanabooru was also eaten in Edo, but the mold with fine cut patterns remains only in Okinawa.
flavor: Baked confection; sensory detail not given in the sources consulted.
craft: The patterned mold is the distinguishing craft element.

name: Kunpen (Ryukyu sesame-peanut baked pastry)
text: Baked Ryukyu confection filled with sesame and peanut butter paste. Used to entertain the Chinese investiture envoys (sappushi) and at memorial services.
craft: Details beyond filling and use were not in the sources consulted.

name: Tannafakuru
text: Baked Ryukyu sweet created as a substitute for kunpen, eaten by commoners.
flavor: Baked sweet; sensory detail not given in the sources consulted.
craft: Contrasted with kunpen's court and ceremonial role.

name: Japanese shortcake (Fujiya and Colombin claims)
ja: 日本のショートケーキ
text: Sponge cake with cream is a Japanese-style shortcake, rarely the main type overseas. Fujiya's FAQ says founder Fujii Rinemon devised it in the Taisho era. The National Diet Library reference entry lists two claims, Fujiya's and Colombin's founder Kadokura Kuniteru; it states Fujiya first sold it in 1922. Fujiya was founded in Yokohama in 1910; its early Christmas cake was fruit cake with dried fruit and liquor. Some sources say 1912 and early butter cream, unverified.
craft: Sources conflict on date and originator.

name: Kakigori history (himuro to Meiji ice shops)
text: Ice houses (himuro) in Tenri, Nara are said to date about 1,300 years, supplying ice to Heijo Palace in summer; Makura no Soshi is the earliest literary source, and it was a privilege. In Meiji, the first ice-water shop opened in Yokohama Bashamichi in 1869 by Machida Fusazo, per one source, though another may confuse it with an 1894 ice shop. Tokyo Seihyo began ammonia ice-making in 1883, ice shaving machine invented 1887, and Tokyo kakigori shops appeared around 1887.

name: Uji kintoki (matcha kakigori with azuki)
text: Kakigori with matcha syrup and sweet azuki, "kintoki" being slang for azuki. Origin uncertain: one account says it was eaten by the Edo period with sugar and matcha sprinkled over ice topped with smooth bean paste; another suggests uji-gori came first and azuki was added.
craft: A story about Tokugawa Ieyasu is told but has no source support.
